title: LOUISVILLE FALL HARVEST FESTIVAL
full_story:
The first event for the 75th Annual Louisville Fall Harvest Festival is tonight when the Rotary Club and Louisville Community Church’s will have a Trunk or Treat on the square from 6 to 7:30 pm.  The Rotary Club will be grilling Salt & Strings Butchery Bub Chops and Blair’s Slaughtering & Processing, Inc pork burgers and hot dogs.

The Kiddie Parade kicks things off Friday afternoon at 2 pm, with Full Armor Christian School serving treats at the old Soda Fountain and the Red Brush Christian Church will be serving apple cider and the Louisville Christian Church will be serving free water near the pocket park.  From 4 to 6 pm the Methodist Church will be offering free chili with Das-zle Dance and tumble performing at 5:30 pm.  From 5:30 to 6:30 pm will be the past Queen reception at the State Bank Suite.  At 6:15 pm Sylvia and Meila Robey will sing on stage.  The Little Miss, JR Miss, and Queen pageants will be held at 7:00 pm.  There are 6 contestants vying for the title of Louisville Fall Festival Queen, The current Queen is Mila Zink.  There are 7 contestants in the JR Miss contest, the current JR Miss is Elsie Anderson, and there are 10 young ladies vying for the Little Miss title held by Landrey Eade.  Mila, Elsie, and Landrey will be the guests today on the ReVue at 2 pm.

The glow 5K Walk, Run will take place after the pageants.  From 9 to 10 pm there will be music on the square with Seth Schnautz.

Saturday starts with the Rotary Pancake breakfast from 7 to Noon, with tickets now on sale.  The FFA, AG Mechanics Tractor show will be on the east side of the square and kids activities will start at 8 am and the Clay County Genealogical Society Library will have an open house.  The Clay County Cruisers Car Show begins at 9, there will also be a greased pig contest, sponsored by the Hoosier Prairie Baptist Church, and a country store will open at the old Clay County Jail with free coffee and popcorn.

The Princess pageant will be on the main stage at 10 am with special guest Briley Mullins performing.  Starting at 11 am will be the Chili Cook Off Contest, hosted by the North Clay FCCLA and the Louisville Chamber of Commerce, with tastings available to 1 pm.  Contestants should bring their chili to the pocket park by 10:45 am.  Sign up by emailing [email protected], the winner will get a $50 prize.  At 11:30 Power and Grace Tumbling will perform on the main stage.  At 1 pm Deputy Trevin Smith and his K9 Chief will have a demonstration.  The parade is at 2 pm, Katrina Van Dyke has been named as the parade marshal.  Following the parade the crowning of the Queens and the Rotary Basket Raffle winners will be announced.

For the Parade floats, cars, tractors, bands and Queens will line up at the grade school, horses will line up at the city park, Louisville Queens and contestants will line up on Magnolia Street, and Emergency Services will line up at the high school.  Handicap parking for the parade will be available on the east side of the square.

All weekend there will be arts, and crafts, food vendors, basket raffle and inflatables for the kids.

In conjunction with the Fall Harvest Festival the Louisville American Legion will have a meat shoot on Sunday, November 1st at 11 am.

title: BLOOD DRIVE
full_story:
The American Red Cross is appealing for blood and platelet donors of all blood types to schedule donation appointments this fall.  The organization provides more than 6.5 million blood products to hospitals nationwide each year.

There will be a Blood Drive tomorrow at the Clay City High School from 1 to 5 pm.  By donating at this drive you help graduating seniors earn scholarships.  All donors will also get a Red Cross t-shirt.

To be eligible to donate, individuals must be at least 17 years old, or 16 with parental consent, where permitted by state law and weigh at least 110 pounds while in generally good health.  High school students and other donors 18 years of age and younger must also meet specific height and weight requirements.  Donors must present a blood donor card, driver’s license or two other forms of identification at check-in.

Appointments can be made using the Red Cross Blood Donor App, by visiting RedCrossBlood.org, by calling 1-800-RED CROSS or by enabling the Blood Donor Skill on Alexa Echo devices.  Donors can use RapidPass online on the day of their appointment to complete pre-donation reading and health history questionnaires before arriving.

The next Blood Drive in our area will be on Tuesday, November 10th at the Oil Belt Christian Service Camp from 1 to 5 pm.

title: SCARECROW CONTEST WINNERS
full_story:
Winners have been named in the Flora Chamber of Commerce annual Scarecrow contest.  There were 10 entries in this year’s contest.

Winning the People’s Choice award was the Scarecrow at First Community Bank with their “UP” display.  The scarecrow is Carl Fredrickson from the Disney movie UP along with his house.  The display wom with 256 likes.  Winning the Mayors Choice was the Scarecrow at WNOI at 1001 North Olive.  The scarecrow recreates the scene from the Dixie Chicks song “Goodbye Earl” complete with musical accompaniment.  There were more than 600 likes or comments on Facebook for the top 2 displays.

Photos of all participating Scarecrows are posted in an album on the Flora Chamber of Commerce Facebook page.  Votes were tabulated Monday evening.

title: FRAN CARTER SCHOLARSHIP FASHION SHOW
full_story:
The Frontier Community College Foundation and Carnaby Square, Fairfield’s “Fashion Leader” are once again teaming up to host the 9th Annual Fran Carter Memorial Scholarship Fashion Show on Sunday, November 8th.

This event is being held at First Christian Church in Fairfield.  “All three entities were close to Fran’s heart, so it is fitting that the church work with the Foundation and Carnaby Square to host the event.”  Doors will open at 2 pm, with the fashion show beginning at 2:30 pm.  Those coming to the fashion show are asked to bring canned goods.

The fashion show highlights fall fashions available exclusively at Carnaby Square as well as tuxedos available for rental.  All tickets must be purchased in advance.  Reserved tables of 8 sell for $100 and individual tickets are available for $15 each.  Drinks and light refreshments will be served.  Tickets can be purchased exclusively at Carnaby Square or through Linda Spicer who can be reached at 217-725-1340.  All proceeds will go the Fran Carter Memorial Scholarship available to second-year student athletes at Frontier.

title: OPERATION CHRISTMAS CHILD
full_story:
Nearly 5,000 drop-off locations for Operation Christmas Child will open soon.

According to a news release, volunteers across the country will be preparing to collect shoeboxes for this year’s Operation Christmas Child, one of the projects of Samaritan’s Purse.  Over the last 33 years, the project has collected and delivered shoeboxes filled with toys, school supplies, and personal care items to millions of children around the world.  Many of those children are suffering from war, poverty, disease and disaster.

For those who wish to participate in this year’s project, you can find a step-by-step guide on the How to Pack a Shoebox webpage.  The project partners with different churches across the world to deliver the boxes once they’ve been collected. You can also donate $10 per shoebox gift online through “Follow Your Box” to receive a tracking label and discover its destination.

“Shoebox gifts may seem simple, but they have an eternal impact.  Each box is an opportunity to tell a boy or girl in need about the true meaning of Christmas,” said Franklin Graham, president of Samaritan’s Purse.  “I’ve delivered these boxes around the world, and I never get tired of seeing the joy that they bring, even in the midst of disasters, war, and poverty.”

Operation Christmas Child has collected and delivered more than 244 million gift-filled shoeboxes and delivered them to children in more than 175 countries and territories.

Collection week is set for November 16 through November 23rd.  In Flora the drop off location is Christ’s Church, packages will be collected Monday, November 16th from 1 to 3 pm and from 5 to 7 pm.  On Tuesday November 17th from 9 to 11 am, Wednesday, November 18th from 1 to 3 pm, Thursday, November 19th from 9 to 11am, Friday, November 20th from 1 to 3 pm and from 5 to 7 pm, on Saturday, November 21st from 10 to Noon, on Sunday, November 22nd from 9:30 am to 1:30 pm and on Monday, November 23rd from 7 to 9 am.

title: HOMESCHOOL STUDENT TUITION DISCOUNT
full_story:
Illinois Eastern Community Colleges is making college courses more affordable for eligible homeschool students through its Early College Homeschool Tuition Waiver, offering tuition discounts of up to 70%.

The waiver is available to in-district homeschool students during their junior and senior years of high school.  Students may receive reduced tuition for up to six credit hours per fall or spring semester, with a maximum of 24 credit hours per student.

“Homeschool students are an important part of our college community, and we want families to know there is a path for them to begin earning college credit,” said Erin Volk, IECC director of dual credit.  “This tuition waiver can help make that opportunity more affordable while giving students a head start on their education and career goals.”

For the 2026-27 academic year, eligible students pay $42 per credit hour for core priority courses and priority career pathway courses, compared with the regular in-district tuition rate of $140 per credit hour.  Elective courses cost $70 per credit hour.

A three-credit-hour priority course costs $126 in tuition, compared with the regular rate of $420.  A three-credit-hour elective course costs $210.

Students may enroll in more than six credit hours per semester, but additional hours are billed at full tuition rates.  All courses carry student fees; some courses may carry additional fees for materials, supplies, insurance or other program needs.  For more information about fees, please see the IECC Course Catalog or request more information when meeting with a director of dual credit.

Priority courses include general education classes aligned with IECC’s Three to Your Degree program, such as composition, college algebra, introductory biology, psychology and public speaking.  Priority career pathway courses align with career and technical degree or certificate programs.

Students can take college courses while continuing their homeschool education.  Courses may serve as individual learning opportunities or be included on a homeschool transcript.

“The right courses depend on where a student wants to go next,” said Megan Black, IECC director of dual credit.  “We can help students explore general education courses for a transfer degree or classes connected to a career and technical program.  Advising helps families understand their options and choose courses that fit the student’s goals and readiness.”

IECC recommends students typically begin college coursework during their junior or senior year, allowing time to develop the academic foundations and study habits needed for success.

Students who have completed eighth grade, are at least 14 and demonstrate college readiness may enroll as nondegree-seeking students.  Eligibility to enroll does not automatically qualify a student for the tuition waiver, which is limited to eligible in-district juniors and seniors.

To get started, students should apply online, submit a transcript signed by the homeschool administrator documenting completion of eighth grade, and complete ACCUPLACER testing to demonstrate college readiness.  Students should then meet with a director of dual credit and complete an advising appointment before registering and arranging payment.  Some courses have additional prerequisites, program admission requirements or age restrictions.

title: IFB ANNUAL MEETING
full_story:
Scott McKain, an internationally recognized keynote speaker, business strategist and bestselling author known for his work on customer experience, differentiation and helping organizations stand out in competitive markets, will be the keynote speaker during Illinois Farm Bureau’s Annual Meeting.

This year’s meeting, with the theme “Farming for the Next Generation,” will be December 12th through 15th at the Hyatt Regency in Chicago.  McKain will speak Saturday night, with the president’s address Sunday morning.

McKain has spent more than three decades consulting and speaking for companies around the world, delivering more than 2,000 keynote presentations on leadership, relevance and creating distinction in business.

McKain is the author of several acclaimed business books, including “Create Distinction,” “ICONIC,” “The Ultimate Customer Experience” and “Beyond Distinction.”  His presentations focus on helping organizations build lasting customer relationships, create unique value and remain relevant in rapidly changing markets.

Illinois Farm Bureau also announced more than a dozen micro talks will be available to meeting attendees December 12th and 13th.  A tradition at Annual Meeting, the talks bring experts and members together to share information on popular agricultural topics.

Attendees can also expect the return of charitable auctions, ice cream fundraiser, Young Leader Discussion Meets and awards programs.

“Annual Meeting provides the IAA Foundation an excellent opportunity to raise funds to further our charitable mission.  We are grateful to members and local businesses who donate items to place on the in-person, online and live auctions, and we are currently seeking additional donations for this year’s lineup,” IAA Foundation Director Susan Moore said.

Anyone interested in donating an item for auction can visit iaafoundation.org for more details or visit your county Farm Bureau. Donations are appreciated by November 2nd.

The deadline to register for Annual Meeting is November 13th.  Contact your county Farm Bureau to register.

title: ILLINOIS HALLOWEEN
full_story:
The state’s farmers produced 532.8 million pounds of pumpkins in 2025, more than any other state in the nation, according to the US Agriculture Department.

Nearly 40% of the nation’s pumpkins came from Illinois, making the state a major contributor to America’s favorite fall traditions.

California ranked a distant second, with 161.7 million pounds, followed by Indiana at 134.8 million pounds.  Illinois produced more pumpkins than those two states combined.

To put Illinois’ pumpkin production into perspective, the state’s annual harvest could theoretically make, 2 billion pumpkin spice lattes, 284 million pumpkin pies, 568 million loaves of pumpkin bread, and 35 million jack-o’-lanterns.

Those estimates use recipe ingredients and average pumpkin weights to show just how far Illinois’ harvest could go.  Actual production includes pumpkins grown for different purposes, including processing and decoration.

Illinois’ pumpkin dominance is nothing new.  Morton, Illinois, is known as the “Pumpkin Capital of the World” because of its role in producing canned pumpkin.  The central Illinois community has helped turn the state’s farmland into a major source of pumpkin products enjoyed across the country.

Illinois’ fertile soil, agricultural expertise and generations of hardworking farmers have helped make that possible.

While Illinois faces plenty of challenges, its agricultural success is something worth celebrating.

From pumpkin patches and Halloween decorations to Thanksgiving pies and fall coffee drinks, Illinois farmers help make the season possible for millions of Americans.
